title: My hair was black
hookLine: Ambapali's song of her aging body: once lovely, now changed; the truth's word never fails (Therigatha, Ambapali)
carry: so it was, so it is

cards: Black as bees, curled at the tips. That's how Ambapali remembers her hair. The path met her before as the courtesan of Vesali who hosted the Buddha for a meal and gave his community her mango grove.
In the Therigatha she is an old nun, and her song walks down her own body, from her hair to her feet, then and now. Every verse ends the same way.

teach.b: First, then and now. My hair was black, she says, the color of bees, curled at the tips. Now, with age, it's like coarse bark fiber.

teach.h: EYES, VOICE, TEETH: THEN AND NOW.
teach.b: Then the refrain: not otherwise is the word of the one who speaks the truth. So it was; so it is. Second, the walk.
She goes on, part by part. Eyes that shone like jewels, now dim. A voice sweet as a cuckoo's in the forest, now faltering.
Teeth once bright, now broken. Each verse holds a then and a now, and each closes with the same line; the repeating is part of the teaching. Third, who is speaking.
This is the woman who, in the sutta of the Buddha's last journey, wouldn't give up a meal with him for all of Vesali, and then gave his community her grove.
A woman who knew what beauty and wealth could buy tells us, steadily, what time did. Fourth, the tone. Some readers hear grief in the song.
Others hear something calmer: no complaint, no shame, only accuracy.
Near the end she says this body is like an old house with its plaster falling away.

teach.h: SO IT WAS, SO IT IS.
teach.b: And the refrain says the Buddha's word holds: things change. In her mouth that isn't a curse. It's a teaching confirmed, by her own skin.

how: Reflection on the body's changes is a traditional Buddhist contemplation, and Ambapali's verses are read in Theravada settings as a picture of impermanence seen in one's own body.

o: truth, the word that always holds
a vow made before a teacher
a beauty that never fades with the years

games.q: Ambapali, then and now: tap the pairs.
p: not otherwise is the truth-speaker's word

s: Ambapali's song is a bitter complaint about growing old
it names each change plainly, and each verse ends: not otherwise is the truth-speaker's word.
every verse of Ambapali's song ends with the same refrain
each one closes: not otherwise is the word of the one who speaks the truth.
her song describes someone else's body
it's her own body, from her hair down, then and now.

games.q: you're Ambapali, old now, looking at hair that was once black as bees. what do you say?
o: grieve what's gone, and stop there.
name it plainly, then and now, and say the truth-speaker's word holds.
look away and talk of something else.
games.why: verse by verse she names each change plainly, then and now, and closes each one: not otherwise is the word of the one who speaks the truth.

practice: Find one old photograph of yourself, on your phone, in a drawer, or from memory, and look at it the way Ambapali looked at herself: hair then, face then, and softly, so it was.
Then feel the body you're in right now, breathing and here, and let so it is sit beside it, with nothing to argue and nothing to praise.

wordCard.voice: Sacca. Truth: the word behind Ambapali's refrain, that the truth-speaker's word holds, as her song walks her own body, then and now. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sacca: truth. Ambapali's refrain calls the Buddha the one who speaks the truth.

carryVoice: Your line: so it was, so it is. No complaint, no shame, just what time did. That's day seven hundred ninety-one.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta: Ambapali's meal and the gift of the grove)
